is or is not acting because of pressure or duress, and
a decision of the Board to refuse an application for a voluntary assisted dying substance authority in relation to a patient.
A review of a reviewed decision—
is to be dealt with as a new hearing, and
evidence or information may be given in addition to, or in substitution for, the information given in relation to the reviewed decision.
If a review application is made in relation to a patient, the patient is a party to the proceeding whether or not the patient is the applicant for the review.
This section applies if a review application is made in relation to a patient.
If the request and assessment process in relation to the patient has not been completed—
the request and assessment process is suspended, and
no further step in the process is to be taken until the review application is decided or otherwise disposed of.
If the request and assessment process in relation to the patient has been completed—
the process for accessing voluntary assisted dying under Part 4 is suspended, and

no step under that Part, including the prescription, supply or administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance, is to be taken in relation to the patient until the review application is decided or otherwise disposed of.

heading.b: Review application taken to be withdrawn if patient dies

block.txt: A review application made in relation to a patient is taken to be withdrawn if the patient dies.
In deciding a review application made in relation to a patient, the Supreme Court may decide that—
at the time of making the first request, the patient had been ordinarily resident in New South Wales for a period of at least 12 months, or
at the time of making the first request, the patient had not been ordinarily resident in New South Wales for a period of at least 12 months, or
the patient has decision-making capacity in relation to voluntary assisted dying, or
the patient does not have decision-making capacity in relation to voluntary assisted dying, or
the patient is acting voluntarily, or
the patient is not acting because of pressure or duress, or
See the definition of pressure or duress in the Dictionary in Schedule 1.
the patient is not acting voluntarily, or
the patient is acting because of pressure or duress, or
a ground to refuse to issue a voluntary assisted dying substance authority exists, or
a ground to refuse to issue a voluntary assisted dying substance authority does not exist.

heading.b: Effect of decision under s 113(a), (c), (e), (f) or (j)

block.txt: If the Supreme Court makes a decision referred to in section 113(a), (c), (e), (f) or (j) on a review application made in relation to a patient—
section 111 ceases to apply, and
if the request and assessment process in relation to the patient had not been completed when the review application was made—the request and assessment process can be resumed, and

if the request and assessment process in relation to the patient had been completed when the review application was made—the process under Part 4 can be resumed, and any step that is authorised under that Part can be taken, in relation to the patient, and
if the Court sets aside the reviewed decision—subsection (2), (3) or (4) applies.
If the reviewed decision set aside by the Supreme Court is a decision of a coordinating practitioner in a first assessment—
the Court’s decision is substituted for the reviewed decision, and

if the outcome of the first assessment would, but for the reviewed decision, have been that the patient was assessed as ineligible for access to voluntary assisted dying—the coordinating practitioner is taken to have made a first assessment assessing the patient as eligible for access to voluntary assisted dying.
If the reviewed decision set aside by the Supreme Court is a decision of a consulting practitioner in a consulting assessment—
the Court’s decision is substituted for the reviewed decision, and

if the outcome of the consulting assessment would, but for the reviewed decision, have been that the patient was assessed as ineligible for access to voluntary assisted dying—the consulting practitioner is taken to have made a consulting assessment assessing the patient as eligible for access to voluntary assisted dying.
If the reviewed decision set aside by the Supreme Court is a decision of a coordinating practitioner in a final review—
the Court’s decision is substituted for the reviewed decision, and
the final review form is taken to include—

if the reviewed decision is a decision referred to in section 109(1)(c)(i)—a statement certifying that the coordinating practitioner is satisfied that the patient has decision-making capacity in relation to voluntary assisted dying, or

if the reviewed decision is a decision referred to in section 109(1)(c)(ii)(A)—a statement certifying that the coordinating practitioner is satisfied the patient is acting voluntarily in requesting access to voluntary assisted dying, or

if the reviewed decision is a decision referred to in section 109(1)(c)(ii)(B)—a statement certifying that the coordinating practitioner is satisfied the patient is not acting because of pressure or duress in requesting access to voluntary assisted dying.
See the definition of pressure or duress in the Dictionary in Schedule 1.

heading.b: Effect of decision under s 113(b), (d), (g), (h) or (i)

block.txt: If the Supreme Court makes a decision referred to in section 113(b), (d), (g), (h) or (i) on a review application made in relation to a patient—
the patient is taken to be ineligible for access to voluntary assisted dying for the purposes of the request and assessment process in relation to the patient, and
if the request and assessment process in relation to the patient had not been completed when the review application was made—the request and assessment process ends, and
if the request and assessment process in relation to the patient had been completed when the review application was made—
the process for accessing voluntary assisted dying under Part 4 ends, and
no step under that Part, including the prescription, supply or administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance, is to be taken in relation to the patient.

heading.b: Coordinating practitioner may refuse to continue in role

block.txt: If, under section 114(2)(a) or (4)(a), a decision of the Supreme Court is substituted for a decision of a patient’s coordinating practitioner, the coordinating practitioner may refuse to continue to perform the role of coordinating practitioner.

A coordinating practitioner who refuses under subsection (1) to continue to perform the role of coordinating practitioner must transfer the role of coordinating practitioner in accordance with section 175.

heading.b: Hearings of Supreme Court to be held in private

block.txt: Hearings of the Supreme Court in relation to a review application must be held in private.
The Supreme Court may give directions about persons who may be present at a hearing in relation to a review application.

If a review application is made in relation to a patient, the Principal Registrar of the Supreme Court must give notice of the application and any decision or order, however described, of the Court in relation to the application to the following—
if the coordinating practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the patient’s coordinating practitioner,
if the consulting practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the patient’s consulting practitioner,
if the role of administering practitioner for the patient has been transferred under section 64(2)—the patient’s administering practitioner,
the Health Secretary,
the Board.
The Board must, as soon as practicable after receiving notice of a review application under subsection (1), give notice of the effect of section 111(2) and (3) to—
each party to the proceeding, and
if the coordinating practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the patient’s coordinating practitioner, and
if the role of administering practitioner for the patient has been transferred under section 64(2)—the patient’s administering practitioner.

heading.b: Coordinating and consulting practitioners to give Supreme Court relevant material

block.txt: After receiving a notice of a review application under section 118(1), a patient’s coordinating practitioner or consulting practitioner must give the Principal Registrar of the Supreme Court—
if the coordinating practitioner or consulting practitioner made the decision the subject of the review—
a statement of the reasons for the reviewed decision, and
other documents and material in the practitioner’s possession or under the practitioner’s control and relevant to the Court’s review of the reviewed decision, or
if the coordinating practitioner or consulting practitioner did not make the decision the subject of the review—documents and material—
in the practitioner’s possession or under the practitioner’s control, and
relevant to the Court’s review of the reviewed decision.
The coordinating practitioner or consulting practitioner must give the Principal Registrar of the Supreme Court the documents and material, including any statement of reasons—
within 7 business days after receiving the notice of the review application, or
within the shorter period ordered by the Court.

heading.b: Supreme Court to give written reasons for decision

block.txt: The Supreme Court must give written reasons for a decision made in relation to a review application.
The Principal Registrar of the Supreme Court must give a copy of the written reasons to the following—
each party to the proceeding,
if the coordinating practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the coordinating practitioner for the patient,
if the consulting practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the consulting practitioner for the patient,
if the role of administering practitioner for the patient has been transferred under section 64(2)—the administering practitioner for the patient,
the Health Secretary,
the Board.
A written transcript of the part of the proceeding in which the Supreme Court’s reasons for the decision are given orally is sufficient to constitute written reasons for the purposes of this section.

heading.b: Published decisions or reasons to exclude personal information

block.txt: If the Supreme Court publishes a decision, or its reasons for a decision, made in relation to a review application, the Court must ensure the decision or reasons are published in a form that does not disclose personal information about any of the following—
a party to the proceeding,
a person who has appeared before the Court in the proceeding,
if the coordinating practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the coordinating practitioner for the patient,
if the consulting practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the consulting practitioner for the patient,
if the role of administering practitioner for the patient has been transferred under section 64(2)—a person to whom the role has been transferred.
Subsection (1) does not prevent the Supreme Court from disclosing personal information about a person referred to in the subsection—
in written reasons given under section 120(1), or
in a copy of written reasons given under section 120(2).
In this section—
personal information includes any information that would disclose the identity of a person.
On a review application, the Supreme Court may make an interim order the Court considers just.
It is an offence under the Crimes Act 1900, Part 5A for a person, for any purpose or requirement under this Act, to—
make a statement or give information the person knows is false or misleading, or
omit anything without which the statement or information is, to the person’s knowledge, misleading.

heading.b: Cancellation of document presented as prescription

block.txt: This section applies if—
an authorised supplier is given a document that is presented as a prescription for a voluntary assisted dying substance, and
the authorised supplier is satisfied the document—
does not comply with section 74, or
is not issued by the coordinating practitioner for the patient to whom the document relates, or
is false in a material particular.
The authorised supplier must—
cancel the document by marking the word “cancelled” across it, and
give the Health Secretary written notice—
that the document has been cancelled, and
the reasons for cancelling the document.
Maximum penalty—imprisonment for 12 months.

heading.b: Contact person to give unused or remaining substance to authorised disposer

block.txt: If a patient revokes a self-administration decision after an authorised supplier has supplied a prescribed substance for the patient, the contact person for the patient must, as soon as practicable and not later than 14 days after the day on which the decision is revoked, give the prescribed substance to an authorised disposer.
Maximum penalty—imprisonment for 12 months.

If a patient who has made a self-administration decision dies and the patient’s death occurs after an authorised supplier has supplied a prescribed substance for the patient, the contact person for the patient must, as soon as practicable and not later than 14 days after the day on which the patient dies, give any unused or remaining substance to an authorised disposer.
Maximum penalty—imprisonment for 12 months.
In subsection (2), the reference to any unused or remaining substance is a reference to any prescribed substance the contact person knows is unused or remaining after the patient’s death.

heading.b: Recording, use or disclosure of information

block.txt: A person must not, directly or indirectly, record, use or disclose information obtained by the person because of a function the person has or had under this Act.
Maximum penalty—imprisonment for 12 months.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the recording, use or disclosure of information—
for the purpose of performing a function under this Act, or
as required or allowed under this Act or another Act, or
under an order of a court or other person or body acting judicially, or
for the purpose of a proceeding under Part 6 or another proceeding before a court or other person or body acting judicially, or
for the purpose of the investigation of a suspected offence or the conduct of proceedings against a person for an offence, or
with the written consent of—
the person to whom the information relates, or
an executor or administrator of the estate of the person to whom the information relates.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the recording, use or disclosure of statistical or other information that is not personal information.

heading.b: Publication of personal information concerning proceeding before Supreme Court

block.txt: A person must not publish information about a proceeding under Part 6 that discloses personal information about the following—
a party to the proceeding,
a person who has appeared before the Supreme Court in the proceeding,
if the coordinating practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the patient’s coordinating practitioner,
if the consulting practitioner is not a party to the proceeding—the patient’s consulting practitioner,
if the role of administering practitioner for the patient has been transferred under section 64(2)—a person to whom the role has been transferred.
Maximum penalty—imprisonment for 12 months.
In this section—
information about a proceeding means information about—
a proceeding before the Supreme Court under Part 6, or
a decision or order, however described, of the Supreme Court in a proceeding under Part 6.
party to the proceeding—see section 108.
publish means to disseminate to the public or a section of the public by any means, including the following—
in a newspaper or periodical publication,
by radio broadcast, television, a website, an online facility or other electronic means.

heading.b: Application of Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1996

block.txt: The provisions of the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1966, Part 5, Divisions 2–4 (the applied provisions) apply, for the purposes of the enforcement of this Act, with—
the modifications prescribed by the regulations, and
other necessary modifications.
A definition in the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1966 of a term used in the applied provisions also applies for the purposes of the application of the provisions under subsection (1).

heading.b: Court to notify Health Secretary of conviction of offence under Act

block.txt: If a court convicts a person of an offence under this Act, the registrar of the court must give the Health Secretary and the Board notice of—
the conviction, and
the penalty imposed.

heading.b: Protection for persons assisting access to voluntary assisted dying or present when substance administered

block.txt: A person does not incur criminal liability if the person—
in good faith, assists another person to request access to, or access, voluntary assisted dying in accordance with this Act, or
is present when another person self-administers, or is administered, a prescribed substance in accordance with this Act.

heading.b: Protection for persons acting in accordance with Act

block.txt: This section applies if a person, in good faith and with reasonable care and skill, does a thing—
in accordance with this Act, or
believing on reasonable grounds the thing is done in accordance with this Act.
The person does not incur—
civil liability for doing the thing, or
criminal liability under this Act for doing the thing.
The doing of the thing is not to be regarded as—
a contravention of professional ethics or standards or principles of conduct applicable to the person’s employment, or
unsatisfactory professional conduct or professional misconduct for the purposes of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law.
In this section, a reference to the doing of a thing includes a reference to an omission to do a thing.

heading.b: Protection for medical practitioner who refers person or seeks information

block.txt: A medical practitioner—
may, despite any other law—
refer a person (a patient) to another person under this Act, and
make a request for a copy of the patient’s medical records, or other information about the patient, to another person under this Act, and
is not liable to any punishment under law because of the referral or request, and

may not be sanctioned, censured or otherwise penalised by an entity whose function is to regulate the professional conduct of the medical practitioner, only because of having made the referral or request.
A person to whom a referral or request mentioned in subsection (1)(a) is made—
may, despite any other law—
examine the patient to whom the referral relates, or
give to the medical practitioner who made the request a copy of the medical records or the information requested, and
is not liable to any punishment under law because of having carried out the examination or having given a copy of the medical records or other information requested, and

may not be sanctioned, censured or otherwise penalised by an entity whose function is to regulate the professional conduct of the medical practitioner only because of having carried out the examination or having given the copy of the medical records or other information requested.

heading.b: Protection for certain persons who do not administer lifesaving treatment

block.txt: This section applies if a protected person, in good faith, does not administer lifesaving treatment to another person in circumstances in which—
the other person has not requested the administration of lifesaving treatment, and
the protected person believes on reasonable grounds the other person is dying after self-administering or being administered a prescribed substance in accordance with this Act.
The protected person is not liable, civilly, criminally or under an administrative process, for not administering the lifesaving treatment.
Without limiting subsection (2), the failure to administer the lifesaving treatment does not constitute—
professional negligence or another contravention of a duty of care that would incur professional liability, or
a contravention of professional ethics or standards or a departure from accepted standards of professional conduct, or
unsatisfactory professional conduct or professional misconduct for the purposes of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, or
a contravention of principles of conduct applicable to the protected person’s employment.
In this section—
ambulance officer means a person employed or engaged, including on a voluntary basis, by the provider of an ambulance service to provide medical or other assistance to persons in an emergency.
lifesaving treatment means—
lifesaving medical treatment, or
life-preserving medical treatment.
protected person means—
a registered health practitioner, or
an ambulance officer, or
a person, other than a person referred to in paragraph (a) or (b), who has a duty to administer lifesaving treatment to another person.
The Voluntary Assisted Dying Board is established.
The Board—
is an agent of the Crown, and
has the status, immunities and privileges of the Crown.
The Board has the following functions—
to monitor the operation of this Act,
to keep a list of registered health practitioners who are willing to assist with voluntary assisted dying, including by—
participating in the request and assessment process, and
prescribing, supplying or administering a voluntary assisted dying substance, and
being present at the time of the administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance,
to make decisions about applications made to the Board under section 17(1),
to make decisions about voluntary assisted dying substance authorities,

to provide to the Minister or the Health Secretary, on its own initiative or on request, advice, information and reports on matters relating to the operation of this Act, including recommendations for the improvement of voluntary assisted dying,
to refer to any of the following persons or bodies any matter identified by the Board in relation to voluntary assisted dying that is relevant to the functions of the person or body—
the Commissioner of Police under the Police Act 1990,
the Registrar of Births, Deaths and Marriages under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1995,
the State Coroner appointed under the Coroners Act 2009, section 7,
the Health Secretary,
the Secretary of the Department in which the Coroners Act 2009 is administered,
the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency established by the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, section 23,
the Commissioner appointed under the Health Care Complaints Act 1993, section 76,
to conduct analysis of, and research in relation to, information given to the Board under this Act,
to collect, use and disclose information given to the Board under this Act for the purposes of performing its functions,
any other function given to the Board by or under this Act or another Act.
The Board, or a member of the Board, must not give the list of registered health practitioners kept under subsection (1)(b), or information on the list, to another entity unless the other entity is—
an official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service, or
a person employed or otherwise engaged by or acting for an official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service, or
another person exercising functions under this Act who needs access to the list or information on the list to exercise the functions.
a coordinating practitioner, a consulting practitioner, an administering practitioner
The Board has all the powers the Board needs to exercise its functions.
The Board may delegate a function of the Board, other than this power of delegation, to—
a member of the Board, or
to a committee established under section 163.
The delegation must be in writing.
A person or committee to whom or which a function is delegated under this section must not delegate the function.

A person or committee exercising a function that has been delegated to the person or committee under this section is taken to do so in accordance with the terms of the delegation unless the contrary is shown.
Nothing in this section limits the ability of the Board to perform a function through—
a member of staff provided to the Board under section 139, or
an agent of the Board.

The Health Secretary must ensure the Board is provided with the staff, services and facilities, and other resources and support, that are reasonably necessary to enable the Board to perform its functions.
The Board, with the Minister’s approval, may appoint a person with special knowledge or skills to assist the Board in a particular matter.
A person who has been appointed to assist the Board may attend meetings of the Board and participate in its deliberations but must not vote at a meeting of the Board.
The Minister may give written directions to the Board about the performance of its functions.
The Board must comply with a direction given by the Minister under subsection (1).
However, a direction under subsection (1) must not be about the performance of a function in relation to a particular person or matter.

heading.b: Minister to have access to information

block.txt: The Minister is entitled—
to have information in the Board’s possession, and
if the information is in or on a document—to have, and make and keep copies of, the document.
However, the Minister is not entitled to have personal information about a person unless the person has consented to the disclosure of the information.
For the purposes of subsection (1), the Minister may—
ask the Board to give information to the Minister, and
ask the Board to give the Minister access to information, and
for the purposes of paragraph (b), make use of staff provided to the Board under section 139 and the Board’s facilities to obtain and give the information to the Minister.
The Board must—
comply with a request under subsection (3), and
make staff and facilities available to the Minister as required under subsection (3)(c).
In this section—
document includes any tape, disk or other device or medium on which information is recorded or stored.
information means information specified, or of a description specified, by the Minister that relates to the functions of the Board.
The Board consists of 5 members jointly appointed by the Minister and the Attorney General by Gazette notice.
The Board must include 2 members who are medical practitioners.
A person may be appointed as a member of the Board if the Minister and Attorney General are satisfied the person has knowledge, skills or experience relevant to the Board’s functions.
A person may not be appointed as a member of the Board if the person—
is an insolvent under administration under the Corporations Act 2001 of the Commonwealth, section 9, or
has a conviction, other than a spent conviction, for an indictable offence, or
is a member of either House of Parliament.
In this section—
spent conviction means a spent conviction under the Criminal Records Act 1991.
The Minister and the Attorney General must appoint—
one member of the Board to be the chairperson of the Board, and
another member of the Board to be the deputy chairperson of the Board.
A member of the Board is not eligible to be appointed as the chairperson or deputy chairperson unless the person is—
an Australian legal practitioner with at least 7 years’ legal practice experience, and
either—
a Judge or other judicial officer, or a former Judge or other judicial officer, of a superior court of record of the State or of another State or Territory or of Australia, or
qualified to be appointed as a Judge or other judicial officer of a court referred to in subparagraph (i).
If the chairperson is unable to act because of illness, absence or other cause or if there is no chairperson, the deputy chairperson acts in the chairperson’s place.
An act or omission of the deputy chairperson acting in the chairperson’s place must not be questioned on the ground that the occasion to act in the chairperson’s place had not arisen or had ceased.
A member of the Board holds office for the term, not more than 3 years, specified in the member’s instrument of appointment.
A member of the Board is eligible for reappointment.
The office of a member of the Board becomes vacant if the member—
dies, resigns or is removed from office under this section, or

becomes bankrupt, applies to take the benefit of any law for the relief of bankrupt or insolvent debtors, compounds with the member’s creditors or makes an assignment of the member’s remuneration for the benefit of the member’s creditors, or
is convicted of an offence punishable by imprisonment for more than 12 months, or
is convicted of an offence under section 158.
A member of the Board may at any time resign from office by written notice given to the Minister or the Attorney General.
The Minister and the Attorney General acting jointly may remove a member of the Board from office on the grounds of—
neglect of duty, or
misconduct or incompetence, or
mental or physical incapacity, other than temporary illness, impairing the performance of the member’s duties, or
absence, without leave, from 3 consecutive meetings of the Board of which the member has had notice.
In this section—
misconduct includes conduct that renders the member unfit to hold office as a member of the Board even though the conduct does not relate to a duty of the office.

heading.b: Extension of term of office during vacancy

block.txt: If the office of a member of the Board becomes vacant because the member’s term of office expires, the member continues to be a member during the vacancy until the day on which the vacancy is filled, whether by reappointment of the member or appointment of a successor to the member.
Subsection (1) ceases to apply if the member resigns or is removed from office under section 146.
The maximum period for which a member of the Board continues to be a member under this section after the member’s term of office expires is 3 months.

If a member of the Board other than the chairperson is unable to act because of illness, absence or other cause, the Minister may appoint another person as an alternate member to act temporarily in the member’s place.
If the deputy chairperson is acting in the chairperson’s place, the Minister may appoint another person as an alternate member of the Board to act temporarily in the deputy chairperson’s place.
While acting in accordance with the person’s appointment, an alternate member of the Board is taken to be, and to have any entitlement of, a member of the Board.
An act or omission of an alternate member of the Board must not be questioned on the ground the occasion for the appointment or acting had not arisen or had ceased.
A member of the Board is entitled to be paid the remuneration and allowances the Minister may from time to time decide.
The first meeting of the Board must be convened by the chairperson, and subsequent meetings must be held at times and places decided by the Board.
A special meeting of the Board may at any time be convened by the chairperson.
A quorum for a meeting of the Board is 3 members of the Board.
The chairperson, if present, must preside at a meeting of the Board.

If neither the chairperson, nor the deputy chairperson acting in the chairperson’s place, is presiding under subsection (1), the members of the Board present at the meeting must elect one of the members to preside.
The Board must decide its own meeting procedures to the extent the procedures are not fixed by this Act.
At a meeting of the Board, each member of the Board present has a deliberative vote unless section 159 prevents the member from voting.
In the case of an equality of votes, the member of the Board presiding has a casting vote in addition to a deliberative vote.
A question is resolved by a majority of the votes cast.

The presence of a person at a meeting of the Board need not be by attendance in person but may be by that person and each other person at the meeting being simultaneously in contact by telephone or other means of instantaneous communication.
A resolution in writing signed or otherwise assented to in writing by each member of the Board has the same effect as if the resolution had been passed at a meeting of the Board.
The Board must ensure accurate minutes are kept of the proceedings at each of the Board’s meetings.

A member of the Board who has a material personal interest in a matter being considered or about to be considered by the Board must, as soon as practicable after the relevant facts have come to the member’s knowledge, disclose the nature of the interest at a meeting of the Board.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.
A disclosure under subsection (1) must be recorded in the minutes of the meeting.
A member of the Board who has a material personal interest in a matter being considered by the Board—
must not vote, whether at a meeting or otherwise, on the matter, and
must not be present while the matter is being considered at a meeting.
A reference in subsection (1) to a matter includes a reference to a proposed resolution under section 160 in relation to the matter, whether relating to the member or a different member.
Section 159 does not apply if—
a member of the Board has disclosed under section 158 an interest in a matter, and
the Board has at any time passed a resolution that—
specifies the member, the interest and the matter, and

states that the members of the Board voting for the resolution are satisfied the interest is so trivial or insignificant as to be unlikely to influence the disclosing member’s conduct and should not disqualify the member from considering or voting on the matter.

Despite section 151, if a member of the Board is disqualified under section 159 in relation to a matter, a quorum is present during the consideration of the matter if 2 members of the Board who are entitled to vote on any motion that may be moved at the meeting in relation to the matter are present.
The Minister may deal with a matter to the extent the Board must not deal with the matter because of subsection (1).

heading.b: Minister may declare ss 159 and 160 inapplicable

block.txt: The Minister may, by written notice, declare that section 159 or 160 does not apply in relation to a specified matter either—
generally, or
in voting on particular resolutions.
The Minister must present a copy of a declaration made under subsection (1) to be laid before each House of Parliament within 14 sitting days of the House after the declaration is made.
The Board may establish committees to assist the Board in the performance of its functions.
The Board may discharge, alter or reconstitute a committee.
The Board may—
decide the functions, membership and constitution of a committee, and
appoint members of the Board or other persons as members of a committee.
The Board may give directions to a committee about its functions and procedures.
A committee must comply with a direction given to the committee by the Board.
Subject to any directions of the Board and the terms of a delegation under section 138, a committee may decide its own procedures.
A member of a committee is entitled to be paid the remuneration and allowances the Minister from time to time decides.

heading.b: Board to send information to contact person for patient

block.txt: The Board must, within 5 business days after receiving a copy of a contact person appointment form for a patient under section 67(4), send information to the patient’s contact person that—
explains the requirements under section 125 to give the prescribed substance, or any unused or remaining prescribed substance, to an authorised disposer, and
outlines the support services available to help the contact person to comply with the requirements.
The Board may ask any person, including a patient’s contact person, to give information to the Board to assist the Board in performing any of its functions.
A person may comply with a request under subsection (1) despite any Act that prohibits or restricts the disclosure of the information.
The Board may, if asked, disclose information, other than personal information, obtained in the performance of its functions to—
a public authority, or
a person or body for the purposes of education or research.

heading.b: Board to record and keep statistical information

block.txt: The Board must record and keep statistical information about the following matters relating to voluntary assisted dying—
the disease, illness or medical condition of a patient that met the requirements of section 16(1)(d), whether or not the patient made a final request,

socio-demographic matters for applicants for voluntary assisted dying, including in relation to age, gender, local government area of residence and, if available, cultural background and level of education,
if a patient has died after self-administering or being administered a voluntary assisted dying substance in accordance with this Act—the age of the patient on the day the patient died,
participation in the request and assessment process, and access to voluntary assisted dying, by patients who are regional residents,
persons assessed as eligible for voluntary assisted dying in a first assessment,
persons assessed as ineligible for voluntary assisted dying in a first assessment,
persons assessed as eligible for voluntary assisted dying in a consulting assessment,
persons assessed as ineligible for voluntary assisted dying in a consulting assessment,
instances of persons being assessed as ineligible for voluntary assisted dying because the persons were acting because of pressure or duress,
the number of voluntary assisted dying substance authorities granted,
the number of voluntary assisted dying substance authorities refused,
the number of times a voluntary assisted dying substance has been dispensed,
the number of confirmed deaths from the self-administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance,
the number of confirmed deaths from practitioner administration of a voluntary assisted dying substance,
the number of instances of an unused voluntary assisted dying substance being given to an authorised disposer for disposal because the patient died before taking the substance,
the number of instances of remaining voluntary assisted dying substance being given to an authorised disposer for disposal because it was left over after the patient died.
a matter specified in a direction under subsection (2).
The Minister may give a written direction to the Board requiring the Board—
to record and keep statistical information about a matter relating to voluntary assisted dying specified in the direction, and
to include the statistical information in its annual report.
The Board must give effect to a direction under subsection (2).

heading.b: Board to notify receipt of forms

block.txt: The Board must, as soon as practicable after receiving a form or a copy of a form from a person under this Act, notify the person that the form has been received.
The Board must, as soon as practicable after receiving a copy of an authorised disposal form or practitioner disposal form, give a copy of the form to the Health Secretary.
A document is executed by the Board if the document is signed on behalf of the Board by 2 members of the Board authorised under subsection (2).
The Board may authorise any of its members to sign documents on behalf of the Board, either—
generally, or
subject to the conditions specified in the authorisation.
A document purporting to be executed in accordance with this section is to be presumed to be executed until the contrary is shown.
The Board must, within 6 months after the end of each financial year, prepare and give to the Minister a report on the operation of this Act during the financial year.
The report must include—
any recommendations the Board considers appropriate in relation to voluntary assisted dying, and
any information the Board considers relevant to the performance of its functions, and
the number of referrals made by the Board under section 136(1)(f), and
the text of any direction given to the Board under section 141(1) or 170(2), and
details of any disclosure under section 158(1) that relates to a matter dealt with in the report and of any resolution under section 160 about the disclosure, and
statistical information the Board is required to record and keep under section 170(1)(b) and (e)–(p), and
statistical information the Board is directed under section 170(2) to include in the report, and

information about the extent to which regional residents had access to voluntary assisted dying, including statistical information recorded and kept under section 170(1)(c), and having regard to the access standard under section 174.
The report must not include—

personal information about a patient, medical practitioner or other person who has participated in the request and assessment process or the process for accessing voluntary assisted dying under Part 4, or
information that would prejudice—
a criminal investigation or criminal proceeding, or
a civil proceeding, or
a proceeding in the Coroner’s Court of New South Wales.
The Minister must ensure a copy of the report is laid before each House of Parliament within 6 sitting days of the House after the day on which the Minister receives the report.

heading.b: Standard about access to voluntary assisted dying

block.txt: The Health Secretary must issue a standard (the access standard) setting out how the Ministry of Health intends to facilitate access to voluntary assisted dying for persons ordinarily resident in New South Wales, including how the Ministry intends to facilitate access to—
the services of medical practitioners and other persons who carry out functions under this Act, and
prescribed substances, and
information about accessing voluntary assisted dying.
The access standard must specifically set out how the Ministry intends to facilitate access to voluntary assisted dying for regional residents.
The access standard may also include information about the potential risks of self-administering or being administered a voluntary assisted dying substance likely to be prescribed under this Act.
The Health Secretary may modify or replace the access standard.
The Health Secretary must publish the access standard on the Ministry of Health’s website.
The coordinating practitioner for a patient (the original practitioner) may transfer the role of coordinating practitioner to another medical practitioner for the patient if—
the consulting practitioner has assessed the patient as eligible for access to voluntary assisted dying, and
the other medical practitioner accepts the transfer of the role.
The transfer of the role may be—
at the patient’s request, or
on the original practitioner’s own initiative.

Within 5 business days after being asked by the original practitioner to accept a transfer under subsection (1), the other medical practitioner must inform the original practitioner whether the medical practitioner accepts or refuses the transfer of the role.
If the other medical practitioner accepts the transfer of the role, the original practitioner must—
inform the patient of the transfer, and
record the transfer in the patient’s medical record, and
within 5 business days after accepting the transfer—
complete the approved form (the coordinating practitioner transfer form), and
give a copy of the coordinating practitioner transfer form to the Board.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.
The coordinating practitioner transfer form must include the following—
the patient’s name, date of birth and contact details,
the original practitioner’s name and contact details,
the other medical practitioner’s name and contact details,
the date the other medical practitioner accepted the transfer,
the date the patient was informed of the transfer,
the original practitioner’s signature and the date the form was signed.
If the other medical practitioner refuses the transfer of the role, the original practitioner may—
refer the patient to another medical practitioner for a further consulting assessment, and
transfer the role of coordinating practitioner to that medical practitioner if the practitioner—
accepts the referral for a further consulting assessment, and
assesses the patient as eligible for access to voluntary assisted dying, and
accepts the transfer of the role.
On accepting the referral for a further consulting assessment, the consulting assessment that previously assessed the patient as eligible for access to voluntary assisted dying becomes void.
If it is not practicable for a patient to make a first request, final request or administration decision in person—
the patient may make the request or decision using audiovisual communication, and

the medical practitioner who receives the request or is being informed of the decision may give the patient advice or information in relation to the request or decision using audiovisual communication.

Subject to subsection (1)(b), a medical practitioner or other registered health practitioner may give advice or information to, or otherwise communicate with, a person for the purposes of this Act using any method of communication, including electronic communication or the use of an interpreter, the practitioner considers appropriate.
However, subsections (1) and (2) do not authorise the use of a method of communication if, or to the extent that, the use is contrary to or inconsistent with a law of the Commonwealth.
In this section—
audiovisual communication means a method of electronic communication designed to allow people to see and hear each other simultaneously.
This section applies to a requirement under this Act for an approved form or other document to be signed.
To avoid doubt, the document may be signed by electronic means.
a digitised signature may be used
However, a written declaration under section 43 may be signed by electronic means only if—
the patient is not able to physically sign the declaration, and
the patient generally uses a digitised signature to sign documents, and
signing the declaration by electronic means takes the form of the patient signing the declaration by using a digitised signature.
An authorised official may make information about voluntary assisted dying publicly available.
Information may be made available under this section using any method of communication, including electronic communication, that the authorised official considers appropriate.
However, subsection (2) does not authorise the use of a method of communication if, or to the extent that, the use is contrary to or inconsistent with a law of the Commonwealth.
The Health Secretary may, by Gazette notice, designate persons, or persons in a class, as authorised officials for the purposes of this section.
In this section—
authorised official means—
the Health Secretary, or
a public service officer employed in the Ministry of Health, or
a person designated as an authorised official under subsection (4).

heading.b: Official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service

block.txt: The Health Secretary may, by Gazette notice, approve an entity to be an official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service for this Act.
The purpose of an official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service is to provide support, assistance and information in relation to voluntary assisted dying to entities, including—
patients, and
patients’ carers, family and friends, and
doctors and other members of patients’ health care teams, and
residential facility managers, and other persons employed or otherwise engaged by or providing services at, residential facilities.
If an official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service is given a list of registered health practitioners kept under section 136(1)(b), a relevant person must not intentionally—
give a copy of the list to another entity that is not also a relevant person, or
disclose information on the list to another person unless the other person—
has requested access to voluntary assisted dying, or
is assisting another person who has requested access.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.
In this section—
relevant person means a person employed by, or otherwise engaged or acting for, an official voluntary assisted dying care navigator service.

heading.b: Health Secretary may approve training, information and other resources

block.txt: The Health Secretary may approve training, information and other resources about the following matters—

the operation of this Act in relation to medical practitioners and other health practitioners, including the functions of coordinating practitioners, consulting practitioners and administering practitioners,
assessing whether or not a patient meets the eligibility criteria,
identifying and assessing risk factors for pressure or duress, including elder abuse and abuse of other vulnerable persons,
See the definition of pressure or duress in the Dictionary in Schedule 1.

matters that will help coordinating practitioners and consulting practitioners comply with the practitioners’ obligations under this Act to provide information to patients about palliative care options,
other matters relating to the operation of this Act.
The Health Secretary may issue guidelines to provide guidance about the request and assessment process.
Without limiting subsection (1), the Health Secretary must issue guidelines about—
the referral by coordinating practitioners and consulting practitioners of patients to medical practitioners under sections 26 and 37, and
the referral by coordinating practitioners and consulting practitioners of patients to psychiatrists, other registered health practitioners and other persons under sections 27 and 38, and
how coordinating practitioners and consulting practitioners may determine whether patients have experienced pressure or duress to request access to voluntary assisted dying, and
the functions and conduct of contact persons.
The Health Secretary may approve forms for use under this Act.
An interpreter for a patient—
must be accredited by a body approved by the Health Secretary, and
must not—
be a family member of the patient, or

know or believe that they are a beneficiary under a will of the patient or that they may otherwise benefit financially or in any other material way from the death of the patient, other than by receiving reasonable fees for the provision of services as the interpreter for the patient, or
be an owner of, or be responsible for the day-to-day management and operation of, a health facility at which the patient is being treated or resides, or
be a person who is directly involved in providing health services or professional care services to the patient.
In this section—
health facility means the following—
a hospital within the meaning of the Health Services Act 1997,
premises where residential care, as defined in the Aged Care Act 1997 of the Commonwealth, section 41-3, is provided,
premises, other than a private residence, where accommodation and personal care or nursing care, or both, are provided to a person with a disability.
interpreter, for a patient, means an interpreter who assists a patient in relation to—
the request and assessment process, or
the process for accessing voluntary assisted dying under Part 4, or
a proceeding under Part 6.

heading.b: Relationship with Guardianship Act 1987 and Powers of Attorney Act 2003

block.txt: To avoid doubt, voluntary assisted dying is not a matter to which the following Acts apply or for which provision may be made under an instrument made under either of the following Acts—
the Guardianship Act 1987,
the Powers of Attorney Act 2003.

heading.b: Annual report to include information about palliative care spending

block.txt: The Health Secretary must ensure that the annual report prepared under the Annual Reports (Departments) Act 1985 for the Ministry of Health for a financial year (a reporting year) includes the following information—
the total amount spent by the Ministry on palliative care during the financial year preceding the reporting year,
the aggregated amounts spent by the Ministry on palliative care during the 5 financial years preceding the reporting year,
the total of the following for the reporting year—
the number of persons to whom palliative care was provided during an admission to a public hospital,
the number of persons to whom palliative care was provided by the public health system other than during an admission to a public hospital.
The information included in the annual report under subsection (1) must be provided—
for the State generally, and
for each local health district.
In this section—
financial year has the same meaning as in the Annual Reports (Departments) Act 1985.
local health district has the same meaning as in the Health Services Act 1997, section 8.
public health system has the same meaning as in the Health Services Act 1997, section 6.
public hospital has the same meaning as in the Health Services Act 1997, section 15.
The Minister must review the operation and effectiveness of this Act, and prepare a report based on the review—
as soon as practicable after the second anniversary of the day on which this section comes into operation, and
after that, at intervals of not more than 5 years.

Without limiting subsection (1), a review of the operation and effectiveness of this Act must include consideration of the principles set out in section 4 including, in particular, the following principles—

a person is entitled to genuine choices about the person’s care, treatment and end of life, irrespective of where the person lives in New South Wales and having regard to the person’s culture and language,

a person who is a regional resident is entitled to the same level of access to voluntary assisted dying and high quality care and treatment, including palliative care and treatment, as a person who lives in a metropolitan region.
The Minister must cause the report to be laid before each House of Parliament as soon as practicable after the report is prepared, but not later than—
for the first review—12 months after the second anniversary, or
for a subsequent review—12 months after the expiry of the period of 5 years.
The Governor may make regulations about a matter that is—
required or permitted to be prescribed by this Act, or
necessary or convenient to be prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Act.
